title: The Painted Zones on a Ship Deck Nobody Stands In
hook: Why will no sailor stand inside these painted lines?
loop: Ends on 'which is why, on every deck in the world, there are painted lines' handing back into scene 2. Pattern A.

scenes.text: On the deck of almost every working ship, there are painted areas the crew will not stand in.
No machinery. No cargo. Just paint.
Is it just caution? A rule written by someone who has never worked a deck?
A moored ship is not sitting still. Wind and current push it constantly against its lines.
Those lines can carry tens of tons of load, hour after hour.
And modern mooring line is not steel. It is synthetic rope.
Synthetic rope is lighter, easier to handle, and it does something steel does not.
A line under heavy load can stretch by several percent of its own length.
And every centimetre of that stretch is stored energy, exactly like drawing back a bow.
As long as the rope holds, nothing happens. The energy simply sits there.
But if the line parts, all of it is released in a fraction of a second.
The ends whip back along the path the rope was pulling.
Faster than a person can see it happen, let alone move.
So crews map those paths in advance, and mark the ground where the ends would travel.
The safest place to stand on a working deck is decided long before the rope ever breaks.
